ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: We received ethics approval by the ethics committee of the Institute of Psychology of the University of Würzburg (reference number: GZEK 2023-66), and the research was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
We conducted two preregistered, randomized between-subjects survey experiments with US participants recruited via Prolific (study 1: N = 399; study 2: N = 396).
Participants read four simulated dialogues in which a patient received medical advice from an AI tool and were randomized to see a disclaimer below the advice or no disclaimer.
All participants provided written informed consent electronically before taking part, were compensated for their efforts and debriefed about the study purpose at the end of the experiment.

We exclusively recruited participants from the US and stratified both samples across gender, age and ethnicity to approximate the composition of the US population (based on a simplified US census, following Prolific's representative-sample procedure).

Fourth, all participants were recruited from the US via an online panel, so the findings may not generalize to other countries, health systems, or populations with different levels of exposure to and experience with AI tools.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Participants were recruited via Prolific. To account for dropout, we preregistered 400 participants as our target sample size for both studies. We exclusively recruited participants from the US and stratified both samples across gender, age and ethnicity to approximate the composition of the US population (based on a simplified US census, following Prolific's representative-sample procedure). Due to a sampling error, we collected data from 404 participants in study 1 and from 400 participants in study 2. All conclusions for study 1 remain unchanged if the four latest datasets are excluded. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 56 columns across 2 data files.
#### Careless Responding

5 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

**What this does not cover.** Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: We conducted two preregistered, randomized between-subjects survey experiments with US participants recruited via Prolific (study 1: N = 399; study 2: N = 396).
Participants read four simulated dialogues in which a patient received medical advice from an AI tool and were randomized to see a disclaimer below the advice or no disclaimer.
All participants provided written informed consent electronically before taking part, were compensated for their efforts and debriefed about the study purpose at the end of the experiment.

We exclusively recruited participants from the US and stratified both samples across gender, age and ethnicity to approximate the composition of the US population (based on a simplified US census, following Prolific's representative-sample procedure).

Fourth, all participants were recruited from the US via an online panel, so the findings may not generalize to other countries, health systems, or populations with different levels of exposure to and experience with AI tools.

#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 3 scripts: 0 ran without error, 0 errored, 3 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **1 script uses an object or function that only another script defines**, so in the second run that script was loaded first, in the same session: `crossexperiment_analyses.R` after `exp1_analyses.R`. Such a script should `source()` the other itself, since it does not run on its own.

**`setwd()` in the code**

**3 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

"(non-literal)", "(non-literal)")), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

text.text: Large language models are increasingly used by the public as a source of medical advice, yet they can produce plausible but incorrect output.
Disclaimers about the limitations of artificial intelligence (AI) are the most common safeguard and are also anchored in regulatory frameworks such as the European Union's AI Act.
Whether disclaimers change how laypeople perceive and act on AI-generated medical advice, however, is unknown.
We conducted two preregistered, randomized between-subjects survey experiments with US participants recruited via Prolific (study 1: N = 399; study 2: N = 396).
Participants read four simulated dialogues in which a patient received medical advice from an AI tool and were randomized to see a disclaimer below the advice or no disclaimer.

Study 1 used the standard disclaimer of a popular chatbot; study 2 used a stronger disclaimer that explicitly highlighted the higher risk of error compared with physicians and required participants to confirm having read it.
Participants rated the advice's empathy, reliability, and comprehensibility and their willingness to follow it.
In study 1, the disclaimer did not significantly affect any outcome (all p > .17).

text.text: In study 2, it did not significantly affect empathy, reliability, or comprehensibility (all p > .19).
text.formatted: In study 2, it did not significantly affect empathy, reliability, or comprehensibility (all p > .19).

text.text: Willingness to follow the advice was slightly lower with the disclaimer (p = .039), but this effect did not remain significant after correcting for multiple testing.
Furthermore, there was no significant difference between the two disclaimers.
Disclaimers may thus serve mainly as transparency and liability measures and should not be relied on alone to protect users.
Alternatives, such as communicating uncertainty within the response and strengthening AI literacy, deserve evaluation.
In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has evolved rapidly, with various applications across healthcare.
AI systems are already used for clinical tasks such as diagnostics, treatment personalization, and gene editing [1].
text.formatted: AI systems are already used for clinical tasks such as diagnostics, treatment personalization, and gene editing <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: In addition to these specialized applications, large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT are an emerging contact point for health-related questions for the general public [2].
text.formatted: In addition to these specialized applications, large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT are an emerging contact point for health-related questions for the general public <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: These tools offer instant feedback and low-threshold access to medical information, which is particularly promising for people with limited access to health care services or financial constraints [3].
text.formatted: These tools offer instant feedback and low-threshold access to medical information, which is particularly promising for people with limited access to health care services or financial constraints <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: They also provide a sense of anonymity compared with face-to-face encounters, which can be especially relevant for stigmatized health issues [4].
text.formatted: They also provide a sense of anonymity compared with face-to-face encounters, which can be especially relevant for stigmatized health issues <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: As LLMs also achieve high diagnostic accuracy in common medical scenarios [5] [6] [7], they could thus help to relieve the strain on our healthcare system.
text.formatted: As LLMs also achieve high diagnostic accuracy in common medical scenarios <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>, they could thus help to relieve the strain on our healthcare system.

text.text: However, other studies highlight significant limitations of LLMs in this context.
In prior studies, diagnostic accuracy was mainly assessed with standardized vignettes or exam questions that contained all relevant information [8, 9].
text.formatted: In prior studies, diagnostic accuracy was mainly assessed with standardized vignettes or exam questions that contained all relevant information <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9]</ref>.

text.text: Such scenarios, however, do not fully reflect the nature of real clinical encounters.
Crucially, more recent studies, which investigated LLM performance in more naturalistic settings, showed substantially worse diagnostic accuracy [10].
text.formatted: Crucially, more recent studies, which investigated LLM performance in more naturalistic settings, showed substantially worse diagnostic accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: A major reason for this discrepancy is suboptimal user behavior.
Users often do not provide enough (or the key) information, which would be required for the model to provide an accurate assessment [10, 11].
text.formatted: Users often do not provide enough (or the key) information, which would be required for the model to provide an accurate assessment <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11]</ref>.

text.text: Due to these obstacles in human-AI interaction, LLMs still frequently provide plausible, but factually incorrect responses.
In medical contexts, reliance on such incorrect information can have serious consequences.
Disclaimers are short notes about the limitations, biases, and potential inaccuracies of AI systems.
Companies often use them for legal reasons, to distance themselves from content and exclude liability [12].
text.formatted: Companies often use them for legal reasons, to distance themselves from content and exclude liability <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: Within the present study, we focused not on this legal function but the informative and warning function: whether a disclaimer changes how users perceive and act on AI-generated medical information.
While intuitively plausible, empirical evidence for such a warning effect is weak.
In a series of studies, disclaimers had no effect on perceived credibility of AI-generated scientific information [12].
text.formatted: In a series of studies, disclaimers had no effect on perceived credibility of AI-generated scientific information <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: Other studies found no effect of limitation disclaimers on trust in a conversational agent [13] or on reliance on AI-generated misinformation [14].
text.formatted: Other studies found no effect of limitation disclaimers on trust in a conversational agent <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> or on reliance on AI-generated misinformation <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: In the only study in the medical context we are aware of, a randomized trial with medical students, a "can make mistakes" warning did not affect responses to AIgenerated diagnostic advice, possibly because students already attributed little credibility to the AI [15].
text.formatted: In the only study in the medical context we are aware of, a randomized trial with medical students, a "can make mistakes" warning did not affect responses to AIgenerated diagnostic advice, possibly because students already attributed little credibility to the AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>.

text.text: How disclaimers change medical laypeople's perception of AI-generated medical advice, however, has not been tested yet.
Since laypeople lack the expertise to critically evaluate the accuracy of medical information, disclaimers may have a stronger influence on them.
Recent regulatory developments have made it necessary to consider how disclaimers affect the perception of AI-generated information.
This especially regards the European Union's AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) [16], which entered into force in August 2024.
text.formatted: This especially regards the European Union's AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>, which entered into force in August 2024.

text.text: It is the first comprehensive law on AI and regulates the development and use of AI systems in the European Union.
Because of this pioneering role and as products must be adapted to EU standards, it is expected to influence AI development globally [17].
text.formatted: Because of this pioneering role and as products must be adapted to EU standards, it is expected to influence AI development globally <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: A central measure of the EU AI Act to protect users from the risks posed by AI is transparency.
First, Article 50 requires that people must be informed when they interact with an AI system and that AI-generated content must be marked as such.
Second, Article 13 requires that high-risk AI systems, which includes medical devices, must be accompanied by instructions for use describing their capabilities, and limitations [16].
text.formatted: Second, Article 13 requires that high-risk AI systems, which includes medical devices, must be accompanied by instructions for use describing their capabilities, and limitations <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>.

text.text: Notably, Article 13 addresses deployers rather than end users, so how information about AI limitations should reach laypeople is left to implementation.

Understanding whether limitation disclaimers affect user perception is therefore relevant for the design of transparency measures and, more broadly, to evaluate the effectiveness of such measures in general.

We conducted two randomized online experiments to test whether a standard disclaimer (i.e., the disclaimer used by Google's Gemini in April 2025; study 1) and a strong disclaimer emphasizing AI risks (study 2) influence the perception of AI-generated medical advice.
We hypothesized that disclaimers would increase awareness of AI's limitations and thereby lower ratings of perceived empathy, reliability, and willingness to follow the advice.
As perceived comprehensibility is a more technical characteristic, no effect was expected for this dimension.
In an exploratory analysis, we further compared both experiments to test whether the strong disclaimer had a larger effect on user perceptions than the standard disclaimer.
Contrary to our hypotheses, neither disclaimer significantly changed participants' ratings or behavior.
Two online experiments with identical structure were conducted sequentially with independent samples.
Participants (study 1: N=399; study 2: N=396) were randomly assigned to a disclaimer or a no-disclaimer condition.
In both studies, they were presented with four simulated dialogues of patients consulting an AI tool for medical advice.
Using established Likert scales, they evaluated the presented advice in terms of perceived empathy, reliability, comprehensibility and willingness to follow.
The key difference between both studies was the wording of the disclaimer (see Table 1).

text.text: We received ethics approval by the ethics committee of the Institute of Psychology of the University of Würzburg (reference number: GZEK 2023-66), and the research was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
All participants provided written informed consent electronically before taking part, were compensated for their efforts and debriefed about the study purpose at the end of the experiment.
Data collection took place from 10 th to 14 th of December 2025 (study 1) and from 5 th to 8 th of May 2026 (study 2).

Both studies were preregistered before data collection (https://osf.io/93n5w/overview?view_only=2ed21149959749119e18e4bbc69ac9b6  https://osf.io/tqw4m/overview?view_only=a5ee1f8236d2492a8a4c6f2e6b58c513)

text.text: Participants were recruited via Prolific.

An a priori power analysis for a linear mixedeffects model with one fixed effect (disclaimer vs. no disclaimer) and two random intercepts (participant and scenario) indicated a required sample size of N=390 to achieve a power of 90% (standardized regression weight β = 0.3, α = 0.05, 5000 simulations, calculated in R with the simr package, v.1.0.11).
To account for dropout, we preregistered 400 participants as our target sample size for both studies.

We exclusively recruited participants from the US and stratified both samples across gender, age and ethnicity to approximate the composition of the US population (based on a simplified US census, following Prolific's representative-sample procedure).
Due to a sampling error, we collected data from 404 participants in study 1 and from 400 participants in study 2.
All conclusions for study 1 remain unchanged if the four latest datasets are excluded.

As preregistered, we excluded participants who failed the attention check (study 1: 5 participants; study 2: 4 participants), leading to final sample sizes of 399 (disclaimer: 183, no disclaimer: 216; gender identities: 197 females, 194 males, 5 non-binary participants, 3 participants preferred to not disclose gender information; age: M = 46.9 years, SD = 16.5 years) and 396 participants (disclaimer: 201, no disclaimer: 195; gender identities: 197 females, 191 males, 7 non-binary participants, 1 participant preferred to not disclose gender information; age: M = 46.1 years, SD = 16.9 years), respectively.
Each participant was presented with four simulated dialogues, each consisting of a medical question posed by a patient and a respective response, labelled as coming from an AIsupported chatbot.
These dialogues were adapted from Reis et al [18] and covered four medical topics (colonoscopy, agoraphobia, smoking cessation, and reflux disease).
text.formatted: These dialogues were adapted from Reis et al <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> and covered four medical topics (colonoscopy, agoraphobia, smoking cessation, and reflux disease).

text.text: The shown questions were constructed and validated by a certified physician and responses were checked for factual accuracy.
In the disclaimer condition, a disclaimer was shown in bold directly below each AI response (see Table 1).
text.formatted: In the disclaimer condition, a disclaimer was shown in bold directly below each AI response (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: In study 1, the disclaimer reproduced the text that Google's Gemini displayed in April 2025.
In study 2, the disclaimer was reworded to emphasize the risks and limitations of AI.
To ensure attention to the disclaimer, participants in study 2 additionally had to tick a box below each disclaimer confirming that they had read and understood it.

After each dialogue, participants rated the advice on four 7-point scales (adapted from Reis et al [18]): empathy (very unempathetic to very empathic), reliability (very unreliable to very reliable), comprehensibility (very difficult to very easy to understand), and willingness to follow the advice (very unwilling to very willing).

text.text: Participants viewed all four scenarios in random order and rated each immediately after reading it.
After the fourth scenario, they were offered the option to save a fictitious link to the AI tool that had supposedly answered the patients' questions.
This question was implemented as a behavioral indicator of willingness to consult AI for medical advice (see Castelo et al [19]).
text.formatted: This question was implemented as a behavioral indicator of willingness to consult AI for medical advice (see Castelo et al <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>).

text.text: As an attention check, participants then were asked whether the advice was labelled as coming from a human physician or an AI chatbot.
In addition, participants in the disclaimer condition were questioned about how the disclaimer had affected their perception of the advice.
Finally, for exploratory analyses, we assessed participants' attitudes toward AI with two questionnaires (the ATTARI-12 [20] and the health care section of the ATTARI-WHE [21])

text.text: Each outcome was analyzed separately with a linear mixed-effects model including disclaimer (dummy coded, disclaimer condition as reference) as a fixed betweensubjects factor and random intercepts for participants and scenarios.
We report unstandardized coefficients (b) as the mean difference in scale points between the no disclaimer and disclaimer conditions, together with 95% Wald CIs (b ± SE*1.96).
Additionally, Cohen's d is reported as an effect size measure.
Because four outcomes were tested per study, we applied a Bonferroniadjusted threshold for statistical significance of p<.0125.
text.formatted: Because four outcomes were tested per study, we applied a Bonferroniadjusted threshold for statistical significance of p<.0125.

text.text: For the exploratory analysis of saved links to the fictitious tool, we calculated a binomial logistic regression (link saved vs. link not saved) with disclaimer condition as predictor; effect sizes are reported as odds ratios (ORs).

To compare both experiments, we combined data from both studies and calculated linear mixed-effects models containing disclaimer, study, and their interaction as fixed effects as well as participant and scenario as random intercepts.
To allow a meaningful interpretation of the results for both fixed effects, these were effect coded (disclaimer = 1 and no disclaimer = -1; study1 = 1 and study2 = -1).
Finally, we tested whether the effect of disclaimers on the four outcomes depended on participants' attitudes toward AI (measured via the ATTARI-12 score and the health care score of the ATTARI-WHE).
Therefore, we calculated two separate ordinary least squares moderation models for each dependent variable (using Hayes' PROCESS macro, model 1).
Simple slopes were probed at the 16th, 50th, and 84th percentiles of the moderator.

text.text: Overall, the disclaimer had no significant effect on any outcome.
Neither empathy, nor reliability, nor comprehensibility, nor willingness to follow the advice differed significantly between conditions.
Exploratory Bayesian analyses mainly support these null findings (empathy: BF₁₀ = 0.34; reliability: BF₁₀ = 0.16; comprehensibility: BF₁₀ = 0.17; willingness to follow: BF₁₀ = 0.15).

Similarly, the share of participants who saved the link to the fictitious AI tool did not differ significantly between both conditions (disclaimer condition: 23.5%, no disclaimer condition: 29.2%), OR 0.75, 95% CI 0.48-1.17, P=.202.
Like in study 1, the presence of the disclaimer did not significantly affect ratings for any dimension (see Table 2 and Fig 1).
text.formatted: Like in study 1, the presence of the disclaimer did not significantly affect ratings for any dimension (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> and Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>).

text.text: Willingness to follow the advice was slightly lower in the disclaimer group than in the no-disclaimer group, but this difference did not remain significant after adjusting for multiple testing.

Again, exploratory Bayesian analyses support these null findings (empathy: BF₁₀ = 0.16; reliability: BF₁₀ = 0.24; comprehensibility: BF₁₀ = 0.13), with inconclusive evidence regarding willingness to follow (BF₁₀ = 1.02).
Also, the share of saved links did not differ significantly between both disclaimer conditions (disclaimer condition: 22.9%, no disclaimer condition: 23.6%), OR 0.96, 95% CI 0.60-1.54; P=.868).
In two randomized experiments (N=795), we found no credible evidence that disclaimers about AI limitations meaningfully change how laypeople perceive AI-generated medical advice.

This outcome held true across various rating dimensions (perceived empathy, reliability, comprehensibility and willingness to follow the advice) as well as for an exploratory behavioral measure (the share of participants who saved a link to the presented AI tool).
Furthermore, this null finding applied to a standard disclaimer (as used by Google's Gemini in April 2025) as well as for a stronger disclaimer, which explicitly highlighted error risk of AI.

Our results are consistent with previous research in other domains showing that disclaimers have no reliable influence on perceptions of AI-generated content [12], trust in conversational agents [13], or reliance on AI-generated misinformation [14].
text.formatted: Our results are consistent with previous research in other domains showing that disclaimers have no reliable influence on perceptions of AI-generated content <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>, trust in conversational agents <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>, or reliance on AI-generated misinformation <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: They also parallel the finding that warnings did not influence medical students' use of AI-generated diagnostic advice [15].
text.formatted: They also parallel the finding that warnings did not influence medical students' use of AI-generated diagnostic advice <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>.

text.text: The present research extends these findings to medical laypeople, who may be particularly vulnerable to misinformation.
For this group, the warning function of disclaimers would be the most important.
As our results show, disclaimers do not shift perceptions of AIgenerated information or related behavioral intentions, even in this setting.
Several explanations for the present null findings are plausible.
Participants may already hold a baseline skepticism toward AI-generated medical advice [18], so a disclaimer (especially the standard disclaimer in study 1) adds little information [15].
text.formatted: Participants may already hold a baseline skepticism toward AI-generated medical advice <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>, so a disclaimer (especially the standard disclaimer in study 1) adds little information <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>.

text.text: This assumption, however, stands in contrast to our exploratory moderation analyses.
These showed that (at least for certain dimensions), disclaimers reduced ratings more, the more negative attitudes people indicated toward AI in general and specifically within healthcare.
Furthermore, disclaimers are now commonly part of AI-generated information, especially for higher urgency cases [22].
text.formatted: Furthermore, disclaimers are now commonly part of AI-generated information, especially for higher urgency cases <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, people may have habituated to such information and no longer pay much attention to it.
We tried to address this issue in study 2 by making participants explicitly confirm that they have read and understood the disclaimer, which however did not change the results.
Nevertheless, it is possible that even in this case, participants did not really process the provided information and perceived it as some kind of "boilerplate".

In line with such reasoning, several participants indicated in the follow-up questionnaire that they believe that the disclaimer mostly serves transparency and liability reasons and they therefore did not pay much attention to it.

From a metacognitive perspective [23], disclaimers may thus trigger monitoring (users register the disclaimer information), without triggering control (users do not adjust how they evaluate the advice).
text.formatted: From a metacognitive perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref>, disclaimers may thus trigger monitoring (users register the disclaimer information), without triggering control (users do not adjust how they evaluate the advice).

text.text: Our findings suggest that limitation disclaimers function mainly as a transparency and liability measure.
However, transparency alone may be insufficient to protect users from the risks of AI-generated medical advice.
This outcome may be critical for AI regulation.
For instance, the EU AI Act establishes transparency as a key measure to protect users from risks of AI use [17].
text.formatted: For instance, the EU AI Act establishes transparency as a key measure to protect users from risks of AI use <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: The result that disclaimers do not change the evaluation of AI-generated medical advice, raises doubts as to whether these measures really fulfil their intended goal.
Policymakers and AI developers should therefore avoid treating disclaimers as a sufficient safeguard and should evaluate transparency measures empirically before deployment.
Furthermore, alternative approaches deserve testing.

A communication style reflecting a certain degree of uncertainty, rather than adding a disclaimer to a confidently phrased answer, lowered trust in AI in earlier work [13] and may encourage more critical use.
text.formatted: A communication style reflecting a certain degree of uncertainty, rather than adding a disclaimer to a confidently phrased answer, lowered trust in AI in earlier work <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> and may encourage more critical use.

text.text: Educating users about how LLMs work could allow for more informed decisions about reliance, although the evidence is nuanced: higher AI literacy was associated with greater trust in one study, whereas medium literacy was associated with more skepticism in high-stakes scenarios [24].
text.formatted: Educating users about how LLMs work could allow for more informed decisions about reliance, although the evidence is nuanced: higher AI literacy was associated with greater trust in one study, whereas medium literacy was associated with more skepticism in high-stakes scenarios <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref>.

text.text: Strengthening metaknowledge, that is, awareness of one's own limitations, may also promote critical use.
The combination of both AI literacy and metaknowledge may enable users to evaluate AI output properly, rather than being excessively skeptical or blindly trusting [25].
text.formatted: The combination of both AI literacy and metaknowledge may enable users to evaluate AI output properly, rather than being excessively skeptical or blindly trusting <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>.

text.text: The present work has several limitations.
First, all advice was verified by a physician and therefore medically accurate.
However, disclaimers may work differently for advice containing (obvious) errors.
Future studies should manipulate the accuracy of the advice, with appropriate ethical safeguards and debriefing about misleading content.
Second, participants evaluated fixed, single-turn dialogues and had to adopt the perspective of another person.
Third, next to our exploratory behavioral measure, all outcomes were self-reported ratings, which can be subject to response biases.

Fourth, all participants were recruited from the US via an online panel, so the findings may not generalize to other countries, health systems, or populations with different levels of exposure to and experience with AI tools.
Across two randomized experiments, neither a standard nor a strong disclaimer about AI limitations affected laypeople's perception of or willingness to follow AI-generated medical advice.
Disclaimers therefore appear to primarily fulfill a transparency and liability function but do not necessarily encourage critical engagement with AI-generated content.
Given the reliance of regulatory frameworks on transparency measures, these findings suggest that disclaimers alone may not provide adequate protection for users.
Future research should evaluate additional approaches, such as communicating AI uncertainty, and explore interventions that strengthen AI literacy and metaknowledge.
